prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.

We represent: petitioner noncitizen.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an Immigration Judge's adverse credibility finding must rest on specific, cogent reasons bearing a legitimate nexus to the finding.

Cite at least six decisions of the Second Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
ARGUMENT

THE ADVERSE CREDIBILITY FINDING CANNOT STAND UNLESS SPECIFIC, COGENT REASONS BEARING A LEGITIMATE NEXUS TO THE FINDING SUPPORT IT.

**A. The governing standard requires reasoned, record-based findings.**

This Court reviews credibility findings for substantial evidence, but deference is not abdication. An Immigration Judge ("IJ") who disbelieves an applicant must give "specific, cogent" reasons that "bear a legitimate nexus" to the finding. *Secaida-Rosales v. INS*, 331 F.3d 297, 307 (2d Cir. 2003) (internal quotation marks omitted), *superseded by statute on other grounds*, REAL ID Act of 2005, Pub. L. No. 109-13, § 101(a)(3), 119 Stat. 231, 303, *as recognized in Xiu Xia Lin v. Mukasey*, 534 F.3d 162, 167 (2d Cir. 2008) (per curiam); *see also Ramsameachire v. Ashcroft*, 357 F.3d 169, 178 (2d Cir. 2004).

The requirement has two components. The IJ must identify what, precisely, undermines the testimony and must show why that matter logically bears on whether the applicant is telling the truth. A conclusory label such as "vague," "implausible," or "inconsistent" does neither unless the record gives it content. Nor can meaningful review occur if the Court must guess which testimony the IJ disbelieved, or why.

**B. The REAL ID Act broadened the permissible grounds but preserved the need for reasons.**

For applications filed on or after May 11, 2005, an IJ may rely on an inconsistency, inaccuracy, or falsehood "without regard to whether" it goes to the heart of the applicant's claim. 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)(B)(iii). To that extent, *Secaida-Rosales* no longer controls. But the same provision requires the IJ to consider "the totality of the circumstances, and all relevant factors." *Id.* This Court accordingly permits reliance on collateral inconsistencies so long as the totality of the circumstances establishes that the applicant is not credible. *Xiu Xia Lin*, 534 F.3d at 167. The statute thus expands what an IJ may consider; it does not excuse the IJ from explaining why the cited matter, viewed in context, casts doubt on the applicant's veracity.

Omissions illustrate the point. Their probative value depends on whether the omitted facts are ones the applicant or witness would reasonably have been expected to disclose in the earlier account. *Hong Fei Gao v. Sessions*, 891 F.3d 67, 78–79 (2d Cir. 2018). An IJ therefore may not treat every later elaboration as evidence of fabrication without examining the context in which the earlier account was given and what it purported to cover. *See id.*

**C. Speculation supplies no legitimate nexus.**

An IJ may draw reasonable inferences, but those inferences must be tethered to the evidentiary record; bald speculation will not do. *Siewe v. Gonzales*, 480 F.3d 160, 168–69 (2d Cir. 2007). A finding that testimony is implausible must likewise rest on more than unsupported assumptions about how people, officials, or persecutors ordinarily behave. *See id.* Where no evidence or reasoned inference connects the IJ's premise to the conclusion that the applicant testified falsely, the required nexus is missing.

**D. Defective reasons require remand.**

When the agency relies on erroneous grounds, this Court asks whether it can confidently predict that the agency would reach the same result absent the errors. *Xiao Ji Chen v. U.S. Dep't of Justice*, 471 F.3d 315, 338–39 (2d Cir. 2006); *see Cao He Lin v. U.S. Dep't of Justice*, 428 F.3d 391, 401–02 (2d Cir. 2005). If it cannot, remand is required. The government may not repair the decision with rationales the agency never offered, and the Court may not supply them on the agency's behalf. *See Cao He Lin*, 428 F.3d at 400; *SEC v. Chenery Corp.*, 318 U.S. 80, 95 (1943).

Each stated reason must therefore be tested for record support and logical relevance, and any surviving reasons must then be weighed under the totality of the circumstances. [Apply this test to each of the IJ's stated reasons, with record citations.] Because the adverse credibility finding fails that test, the Court should grant the petition, vacate the agency's decision, and remand.
